chapter.name: Economic Activities Around Us
chapter.blurb: Chapter 14, the final chapter of the book, explains how economic activities are classified into three broad economic sectors -- primary, secondary and tertiary -- building on Chapter 13's distinction between economic and non-economic activities. Primary sector activities (agriculture, mining, fishing, raising livestock, forestry) draw goods directly from nature; secondary sector activities (construction, manufacturing, utilities) transform those raw materials into finished products, illustrated with a 2022 Indian automobile-production table; and tertiary sector activities (transport, trade, healthcare, education, banking and similar services, also called the service sector) support people working in the other two sectors. A central case study traces the true story of AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited), founded in 1946 under Tribhuvandas Patel and Dr. Varghese Kurien after Gujarat's dairy farmers, tired of exploitative middlemen, took Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's advice to form a cooperative -- showing milking (primary), processing into butter and milk powder (secondary), and transport and retail (tertiary) as one interconnected chain. A second, shorter example follows the same three-sector journey from wood pulp to a printed textbook, alongside paper-recycling facts, before the chapter's closing 'Before we move on' summary ties the three sectors' difference and interdependence together as the book's final teaching point.

scope_in.item: Chapter 13's recap that economic activities are those that create monetary value, distinct from non-economic activities; the chapter's opening quotation on the roots of prosperity being economic activity, from Kautilya's Arthashastra; the glossary definitions of 'Monetary value' and 'Economic Sectors'; how the number and diversity of economic activities has grown over time, from earlier activities such as agriculture, livestock rearing, tool production, pottery and weaving cloth to today's diverse activities such as manufacturing computers/mobile phones/drones, banking, schooling, hotels, transportation, furniture-making, tailoring, software creation and appliance repair; and the chapter's three 'Big Questions' (how economic activities are classified, what differentiates them into sectors, and how the three sectors are interconnected)

The definition of economic sectors as broad groups formed by classifying together economic activities that share similar characteristics; the three main types -- primary, secondary and tertiary economic sectors; and the sector-map illustration on page 197 grouping Agriculture, Mining, Fishing, Raising livestock and Forestry under the primary sector, Construction, Manufacturing, Water supply, Solar power and Electricity production under the secondary sector, and Healthcare, Trade and logistics, Communication, Banking and Transportation under the tertiary sector

The definition of primary sector activities as those in which people are directly dependent on nature to produce goods; the most common primary activities named (agriculture, mining, fishing, raising livestock, forestry); worked examples (cultivating grains/vegetables, collecting wood, extracting coal, catching fish, collecting eggs from poultry farms); and the named picture examples (raising livestock, greenhouse farming, mining, fish farming/fishery, forestry)

The definition of secondary sector activities as those in which people depend on outputs of the primary sector and transform them to produce goods, including construction, utilities (water, electricity, gas) and factory manufacturing; worked examples (processing grain into flour, extracting oil from groundnut, processing tea leaves, wood into furniture and paper, cotton into cloth, steel from iron ore into automobiles); the named picture examples (automobile factory, textile factory, pharmaceutical factory, furniture production unit); and the 2022 Indian automobile-production table (passenger vehicles 45 lakh, commercial vehicles 10.3 lakh, three wheelers 8.6 lakh, two wheelers 2 crore), sourced to the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers

The definition of tertiary sector activities as those that provide support to people involved in primary and secondary activities, including services that may not be directly visible; worked examples (a truck driver transporting produce, fruit/vegetable vendors, doctors, nurses, teachers, lawyers, pilots, technicians, mechanics, electricians, communication services, software development, and services at hotels/restaurants/banks/schools/hospitals/airports/shops/warehouses); its alternate name, the service sector; and the glossary definitions of 'Tertiary Sector' and 'Warehouses'

The framing of 'Interdependence Among Sectors' as the three sectors playing a role in converting natural raw materials into finished products, introduced through an imaginary excursion to a village in Anand district, Gujarat

The full AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited) story: farmers' present-day practice of selling milk to a nearby dairy and being paid monthly by quantity and quality; the situation roughly 50 years earlier in the early 1940s, when farmers sold milk to neighbouring villages and depended on middlemen who bought milk in bulk at meagre prices, leaving farmers feeling cheated; the farmers' approach to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and his advice to form a cooperative; AMUL's founding in 1946 under Tribhuvandas Patel (lawyer and freedom fighter) and Dr. Varghese Kurien (an engineer who was working at a dairy factory in Mumbai); the cooperative bringing farmers, including women, together with joint control over production, pasteurisation and sale, shared tasks and rising income; the growth that led to a factory in Anand producing butter and milk powder, and eventually a wide product range sold nationally and exported abroad; and the glossary definitions of 'Dairy', 'Cooperative', 'Middlemen', 'Pasteurisation', 'Factory', 'Retail' and 'Export'

The chapter's explicit sector-tagging of each stage of the AMUL story -- milking cows/buffaloes to sell milk as a primary sector activity because the product comes directly from a natural source; processing milk into milk powder, ghee, cheese and butter in factories as a secondary sector activity; and AMUL's transportation (by lorry, truck, rail, air and ship), trading and retailing of its products as a tertiary sector activity -- and the named list of other Indian milk-cooperative brands and their states (Nandini/Karnataka, Mother Dairy/Delhi-NCR, Aavin/Tamil Nadu, Vijaya/Andhra Pradesh, Kevi/Nagaland, Sudha/Bihar, Verka/Punjab)

The book-production illustration (Figure 14.1) showing the transformation of pulp (wooden fibre of a tree) into paper and, after printing, into textbooks; the chapter's statement that none of this would have been possible without all three sectors working together; and the 'Let's Explore' instruction to label Figure 14.1's pictures as primary, secondary or tertiary sector

The paper-recycling facts given in the 'Don't Miss Out' box: recycling one tonne of paper saves 17 trees and 2.5 cubic metres of landfill space, and takes 70 per cent less energy and water than making new paper from wood pulp

The chapter's closing 'Before we move on' summary: that the chapter taught the three sectors of economic activities, and that its examples and illustrations helped show both the difference between, and the interdependence among, the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors

scope_out.item: GDP, national income, each sector's contribution to India's GDP or workforce/employment, and any organised/unorganised or formal/informal sector distinction, quaternary or quinary sectors
scope_out.reason: The chapter defines and uses only the three sectors -- primary, secondary and tertiary -- and gives no GDP figures, employment statistics, or organised/unorganised distinction anywhere in its text; introducing them would pull in a later-grade economics syllabus this book does not cover here

scope_out.item: The White Revolution, Operation Flood, the National Dairy Development Board, or the title 'Father of the White Revolution' for Dr. Varghese Kurien, and any biographical detail about Kurien or Tribhuvandas Patel beyond what the chapter itself states
scope_out.reason: The chapter never uses any of these terms; it identifies Kurien only as 'an engineer who was working at a dairy factory in Mumbai' and Tribhuvandas Patel only as 'a lawyer and freedom fighter' at the time AMUL was founded in 1946

scope_out.item: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's wider political career -- the independence movement, integration of princely states, or the title 'Iron Man of India'
scope_out.reason: The chapter mentions him only once, in the single role of a 'prominent national leader' whom the Anand farmers approached, and who advised them to form a cooperative; it gives no other biographical detail

scope_out.item: Exact figures for AMUL's present-day revenue, membership numbers, milk volumes collected, or any rupee price or wage at any point in its history
scope_out.reason: The chapter never states any of these numbers; the only numeric data anywhere in the chapter is the 2022 Indian automobile-production table under the secondary sector

scope_out.item: The precise visual content of Figure 14.1 beyond its captioned description (pulp to paper to, after printing, textbooks) -- specifically, which individual picture in the figure is meant to represent which of the three sectors
scope_out.reason: The chapter's own 'Let's Explore' activity leaves this labelling as an open exercise for the reader rather than stating it as fixed text, and the extracted page text cannot verify the figure's visual content beyond its caption

scope_out.item: The open-ended 'Think About It' and 'Let's Explore' prompts (e.g. naming primary/secondary activities one has seen, listing neighbourhood economic activities and drawing dependency arrows, naming a local cooperative) and the closing 'Questions, activities and projects' (e.g. illustrating sector interdependence with a flow diagram)
scope_out.reason: These are discussion, activity or project prompts without one single fixed correct answer; where a prompt points to a specific stated fact, that fact is tested directly instead of the open-ended question around it

scope_out.item: Chapter 13's own content ('The Value of Work') beyond the one-line recap that it distinguished economic from non-economic activities
scope_out.reason: Chapter 13 is a separate chapter with its own scope record; Chapter 14 only recaps that one distinction in its introduction before moving on to sector classification

scope_out.item: Any milk cooperative other than the seven named in the chapter (Nandini, Mother Dairy, Aavin, Vijaya, Kevi, Sudha, Verka), or their founding years or further detail
scope_out.reason: The chapter names only these seven brands and their states, in a single 'Don't Miss Out' sentence, with no founding dates or other detail given

concepts.name: Economic activities and the three economic sectors
concepts.description: How the growing variety of economic activities is grouped into broader economic sectors, and the chapter's three Big Questions.
concepts.idea: As societies progress, the number and variety of economic activities through which people earn a living keeps increasing, so grouping similar activities together into economic sectors helps us understand how they function and how they are linked.
concepts.rule: Economic activities that share similar characteristics are classified into broader groups called economic sectors; the three main types are the primary, secondary and tertiary economic sectors.
concepts.example: Chapter 14 opens by asking three Big Questions: how economic activities are classified, what differentiates them into sectors, and how the three sectors are interconnected.

questions.q: A classmate says, 'This chapter's three Big Questions are all about the same single idea, so listing three is unnecessary.' Evaluate this claim using the chapter's own three Big Questions.
questions.a: This claim does not hold up well. Each addresses a different stage of understanding sectors -- classification, differentiation, and interconnection -- so treating them as one repeated idea misses what each question specifically investigates.
s: Rejects or substantially qualifies the claim rather than accepting it outright
States at least two of the three Big Questions accurately
Explains that the three questions address different stages/aspects (classification, differentiation, interconnection) rather than repeating one idea

The AMUL story showed how milk moves from a farmer's cow, through a cooperative's factories, to shops across the country, while the story of how a textbook is made showed the same idea using pulp, paper and printing.'
s: Correctly names/recaps the AMUL story as one worked example of interdependence
Correctly names/recaps the book/pulp-paper-textbook story as the second worked example
Written in a short, coherent 'Before we move on'-style closing-note format
